tagline.text: A remote Babuyan island of limestone beaches and the home of the Calayan rail

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱6,600–12,000 (per person, 4 nights 5 days from Manila)

children.text: Calayan Island is the largest island in the Babuyan group north of Luzon, known for limestone beaches such as Sibang Cove, waterfalls and caves, and the Calayan rail, which lives nowhere else. Regular transport is unreliable, so this is an adventure destination that needs spare days in your schedule.
Calayan Island is the main island of the Babuyan Islands in the Luzon Strait, north of Luzon, and covers about
196 km²
. It is separated from Batanes by the Balintang Channel and belongs to the municipality of Calayan in Cagayan. The highest point is Mount Calayan, a former volcano about
high, and the island's character comes from a forested central ridge, hills, four rivers and a rocky coast of white sand beaches. The population in 2020 is reported to be about 9,600.

What made the island famous is the Calayan rail, identified as a new species in 2004. This flightless bird lives only on this island and is classified as vulnerable. The name comes from the Ibanag language, a mission was founded in 1722, and the island was occupied by American forces in 1940 and Japanese forces in 1941. In 1981 the navy warship BRP Datu Kalantiaw ran aground on the island's coast during Typhoon Clara.
The climate is wet, with annual rainfall reported at about

, heavy rain in November–December and exposure to typhoons. That makes timing and schedule decisive for a successful trip. In calm March–May, boats run relatively reliably, but from September to February the amihan (northeast monsoon) makes the sea rough and cancellations are frequent.

The island has no large resorts, only homestays, small inns and local home cooking. Cash is essential, electricity and mobile signal are limited, and not knowing when the boat will sail is part of the experience. In return, uncrowded beaches, hills with 360-degree sea views, caves and waterfalls easily fill two or three days.

A wide cream-colored beach backed by limestone cliffs and blue-green water, this is Calayan's signature beach. Ancient burial grounds lie around Sibang Cove, and the local government has considered developing it for ecotourism and whale watching. There are rip currents and no lifeguards, so be careful when swimming. Quieter Caniwara Cove and Cababaan Cove lie in the same direction.

A grassy hill next to Sibang Cove with 360-degree views of the Luzon Strait, an old lighthouse and free-roaming goats and cows. The wind is strong and there are no safety rails at the cliff edge, so climb carefully around sunset. The climb is said to take about
20 minutes
A viewpoint close to town overlooking Calayan Airport and the sea, with a cross marker. Entry including an escort guide is reported to be about ₱50.
A sea cave reachable only by boat, with a natural pool fed by freshwater seepage. Whether you can enter depends on waves and weather. There is also a spot nearby used for cliff jumping.
A waterfall reached by a short hike, or by boat to a landing followed by a walk of about
10 minutes
. A boat tour combining Lusok Cave and Magsidel on the same trip is the usual way.
Caanawan Falls is reached by a muddier, deeper trek inland, and Kannaway Cave, between the villages of Dilam and Dibay, has a subterranean pool. A guide is required for inland routes.
A spot where you jump from rocks or swim around a rock to a hidden cove, and a local guide must go with you. Let your guide judge the tide and waves.
The place to meet the island's most special wildlife is Longog Sanctuary. To look for the bird you need to hire a wildlife-tracking guide separately, and you must keep your footsteps quiet.
Take a GV Florida bus from Manila (Sampaloc) to Claveria. The ride takes about
12–14 hours
Arrive in Claveria at dawn, take a tricycle to Taggat Port and sign your name on the PCG passenger manifest.
Cross to Calayan on a lampitaw (a small motorized outrigger boat). In calm seas it takes about
4–6 hours
, so you arrive by midday and, after lunch, visit Sibang Cove and Nagudungan Hill.
Take a boat tour around Lusok Cave, Bataraw Falls and Magsidel, and return to your homestay around sunset.
See Malansing Falls, Caniwara and Cababaan Coves and Sibang Cove beach by boat and on land, then rest on the hill at sunset.
Return to Claveria by lampitaw at dawn, then continue by van and bus to Laoag or Manila.
Leave 1–2 spare days in case of cancellations. A short weekend trip is not realistic.

items.title: Relaxed route
items.subtitle: 3 days on the island plus a nearby island

children.text: After arriving, see Sibang Cove, Nagudungan Hill and the Bangaan viewpoint near town.
With an inland guide, visit Caanawan Falls or Longog Sanctuary and enjoy the birds and forest.
If the weather is good, try the triangle boat tour of Babuyan Claro with Smith Volcano and Chinteb a Wasay (₱8,000–10,000 for the whole boat).

items.title: From Manila by bus and boat (standard)

children.text: Take a GV Florida bus from Sampaloc or Kamias in Manila to Claveria, about
12–14 hours
, with deluxe fares reported at about ₱800–1,150. Leave at 3–4 PM and you arrive at dawn.
From Taggat Port in Claveria, the lampitaw to Calayan takes about
4–6 hours
and costs about ₱650–800 (₱500 in some sources).
Boats have no fixed timetable and leave between 5 and 7 AM, with boarding on the spot. Be at the port by 4:30 AM. Every passenger signs the Coast Guard (PCG) manifest.
Fares change with diesel prices. Confirm with local boat contacts before you leave.
Fly from Manila to Laoag (LAO) or Tuguegarao (TUG), then take a van or bus to Claveria, about
3–4 hours
and about ₱100–300.
Calayan Airport has been operating since 2019, and some sources say small-aircraft flights run from Laoag and Tuguegarao about twice a week. Schedules and booking methods change, so be sure to check.
Boats also leave from Aparri Port, taking about
6–7 hours
or more, at about ₱650–800.
Accounts say the M/V Eagle Ferry from San Vicente Port (Santa Ana) runs irregularly, so checking the schedule is essential.
In the northeast monsoon season, the crossing can stretch to
7–9 hours
A day charter of a habal-habal (motorcycle taxi) costs about ₱1,000–1,500.
Chartering a coastal boat costs about ₱2,500–3,500 per boat.
Inland guides cost ₱300–500 per day, and a guide is required for waterfalls and caves.

On Calayan, the sea decides everything. The best time is March–May, when the sea is calm and dry and boats are most dependable. June–July brings early rains and variable conditions, and August is the peak of the habagat (southwest monsoon), which makes it risky.

From September to February is the amihan season, when waves are high and cancellations frequent. If you go then, plan 1–2 spare days. In the peak months of April–May rooms fill fast, so contact the bus, homestay and boat operators in February–March.

Lodging is mainly homestays and small inns in town and in Dadao. TPS Homestay (JP Rizal Street), Pagdagusan Homestay, Villa Inocencia Inn and San Jose Inn are around ₱200–250 per person, and Apollo Beach Resort in Dadao is said to start at about ₱500. Contacts and rates change often, so check with the tourism office. In April–May rooms fill quickly.

Food is home cooking at homestays and small eateries, at about ₱100–150 per meal. A basic bowl of miki noodles at Olen's Miki House is reported at about ₱40. If you want fish and seafood, tell your host in advance. There is no market and the supply of fresh food is limited.

Electricity comes from a solar hybrid system that aims for 24-hour supply, but outages are frequent, and mobile signal is only weak Smart coverage in town. There are no ATMs or card terminals and GCash is unreliable, so bring all your money and your emergency reserve in cash.
Bring a dry bag or plastic covers so your luggage does not get wet on the dawn lampitaw.
Be at the port by 4:30 AM and get your boat contact in advance.
Bring plenty of cash, and set aside ₱3,000–5,000 separately as an emergency reserve.
Electricity and signal are unreliable, so bring a power bank.
Single-use plastic is banned on beaches and trails, so bring a reusable tumbler.
Do not bargain too hard on boat and motorcycle fares. People on the island depend on visitor income.
Bring enough of your own medicine. The health center has only basics.
Build 1–2 spare days into your plans and book return flights allowing for possible cancellations.
Calayan is an island where weather can strand you for days. Allow slack for your return trip and important plans.
Signing the passenger manifest is mandatory. In an emergency, save the Calayan Coast Guard (PCG) station number 0999-924-3554.
Sibang Cove has rip currents and no lifeguards, so be especially careful when swimming.
Nagudungan Hill is windy and has no railing at the cliff edge.
Do cliff jumping only with a local guide, after checking the tide and waves.
Flights and boat schedules change often. Check the latest information with the Calayan tourism office or boat operators.
An active volcanic island reached by chartering a boat from Calayan. There is no regular transport, so it is usually visited on the triangle boat tour, and the sea must be calm.
A marine reserve and lighthouse island at the northeastern tip of mainland Cagayan, good to combine before or after a Calayan trip.
The island province to the north across the Balintang Channel, a separate trip from Calayan.
The main city of Ilocos Norte, the starting point for the overland route to Claveria.
